doc.title: Laurence Juber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Glasgow, Scotland, July 27, 2016 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Guitar history and the classical divide
title: Upcoming concerts, Martinfest and pin bridges; Bucky Pizzarelli
summary: He describes his upcoming concerts in London and Nazareth, the pin bridge heritage, and a Bucky Pizzarelli album.

story.theme_name: Still working: current gigs, upcoming projects and plans
story.community_name: What's next: upcoming tours, records and plans

blocks.x: ensemble, and the professional parameters of gigging, of making a living doing it — but also, when I refer to the real work starting — I mean Monday night next week I have a solo concert. And it’ll be a two hour concert. Whereas tomorrow night it’s 45 minutes and it’s like okay, the youth orchestra is on next. It’s stacked programming, like a festival. But when I have a solo concert — you know I’ve written 150 pieces for guitar. I’ve arranged probably that many again. You know I have to choose my repertoire based not on the pedagogy of it, but on the entertainment value of it. Tuesday night I’m playing the Pizza Express Jazz Club in London, and my guest guitar player is Nicholas Fitch, who is the current guitar player with NYJO, with the National Youth Jazz Orchestra. So we’re bridging the generations. And we’re going to play Chick Corea’s “Spain” and with two guitars it’ll be a lot of fun. And we’ll do some standards together, and then he’ll do a few solo tunes and I’ll do it myself. And the next night I have a rhythm section. I have two — a great English jazz drummer, Steven Keogh, and Arnie Somogyi the bass player. And we’ll do some trio stuff. And then I fly back to the states and go to Nazareth, Pennsylvania, where Martin Guitars is based, and I’m headlining their Martinfest. So it’s like I’m going from a kind of London jazz context to East Coast American guitar company that has been in business since 1833, has its roots in a Vienese guitarmaking tradition, which still, my guitar, as many acoustic guitars do, have a pin bridge. As opposed to the tie bridge on the classic nylon string, where they tie the string around the bridge. And the pin bridge is a pin that holds the string in place on the bridge. That goes back to Vienna. That goes back to Stauffer. That’s not a modern invention. And what I go for when they build a guitar for me is to try to link back to that tradition, to bring it back to the roots of the six string guitar. Because that really started in the 1770s. Before that the Baroque guitar was basically like a giant ukulele.
Well your career reminds me of Bucky Pizzarelli, who I’ve got to know fairly well. And what’s next, what’s tomorrow.
I have an album, a vinyl album of Bucky Pizzarelli with a group of other guitar players doing arrangements of Bix Beiderbecke’s piano pieces, “In a Mist.”
